reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material assembled here does not include a measured adoption rate for AI in defense, and no Census figure appears in it, so the honest starting point is that these sources describe the procurement and intelligence infrastructure around defense AI rather than how widely it is used. What they do show is where the record lives. Per SAM.gov, the government's own system is the primary record of federal contract opportunities, awards, and subcontract reports, and it is free and searchable. Per FPDS, the Federal Procurement Data System is the underlying transaction-level record of contract actions and vendor performance history, and per USAspending, every federal award is downloadable, built on that same feed.

The mechanics of that record are shifting. SAM.gov reports that the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature has been retired and that contract award searches should be conducted in SAM.gov, with the FPDS ATOM Feed to be retired later in FY 2026. It also reports that the General Services Administration retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System, with subcontracting reporting now available in SAM.gov, and that revisions to ISR eligibility logic in the Subcontracting Plan Reporting system on June 9, 2026 may cause contractors to observe an increased volume of contracts and subcontracts in their Eligible Workspace, which the page notes does not automatically mean anything further. Federal users can still manage contract award records with legacy FPDS credentials. SAM.gov also states plainly that the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and is for official use only.

On the demand side, the Defense Innovation Unit describes its mission as converting entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power, and the site's own framing places it as the commercial on-ramp where commercial AI enters Department of Defense programs. Govini, described here as the defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department, says its platform layer transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources, and the site notes it tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending. The page's own scope statement names decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record.

For the defense-industrial base, Janes describes itself as an open source defence and security intelligence provider that uses vetted on-the-ground and industry specialists as human sensors, verifies every data point against vetted sources, peer reviews final content, and maintains what it calls the largest global dataset of its type, positioned for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. The site labels Janes and Forecast International as subscription sources named for completeness. Silicon Valley Defense Group is described here as a nonprofit monitoring the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security and mapping the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space, though the excerpt harvested from its page contains no substantive text.

The one adjacent category the material does document is government labs. The site's Government Labs section carries two individually verified organisations, each classified against a document the organisation published about itself. Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models, while Shanghai AI Laboratory is backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page's point is structural: state-funded labs draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build, and they can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical takeaway from these sources is narrower than the sector's reputation suggests. There is no ROI evidence reported here, no adoption percentage, and no regulatory posture beyond the handling rules attached to the procurement systems themselves. What exists is an unusually transparent paper trail: solicitations, awards, and subcontract reports on SAM.gov, transaction-level contract actions on FPDS, downloadable award data on USAspending, and a commercial entry point through DIU. A vendor or buyer can trace who is buying what, from whom, before committing, and should treat the Controlled Unclassified Information handling requirements as a condition of participating at all.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogs two government AI labs: Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China. According to the page, each classification is verified against a document the organization published about itself, with the source and date recorded, rather than assigned by keyword, model, or parent-company inheritance. The page notes the two labs represent different political economies: TII operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has released open models at the frontier of research, while Shanghai AI Laboratory is backed by national ministries and municipal government. Both institutions can, in principle, command infrastructure commitments such as compute and facilities that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
